If you rode in a yellow cab in New York City in 2014, details of that ride—date, time, payment, tip—were recorded. After a Freedom of Information Law request by Chris Whong, all 173 million trips on 2014 were released publicly.[^1] What began as curiosity has become a case study of privacy risks in public data: without careful protections, anonymous data is not always anonymous.

[^1]: Chris Whong FOIL post: https://chriswhong.com/open-data/foil_nyc_taxi/

Importantly for every trip, the taxi cab data set includes the drivers medallion and hack license number. This inclusion allows rich cab-level analysis: where do drivers have the quickest customer turnaround or how many trips can a driver make in one day? However, as identified by computer scientist Vijay Pandurangan, the anonymization of these values held a crucial error.[^2]

[^2]: Vijay Pandurangan de-anonymization post: https://medium.com/vijay-pandurangan/of-taxis-and-rainbows-f6bc289679a1

Both the medallion number and hack license numbers are stored in the dataset as an MD5 hash, where every input returns the same output. While this may be effective to anonymize some unpredictable information, both hashed inputs are significantly patterned. For example, license numbers are six or seven digits, and medallion numbers adhere to specific constraints—combined, there were 22 million possible combinations. Within two minutes, using powerful computing, Pandurangan computed these hashes. Within an hour, the entire dataset was de-anonymized.[^3]

[^3]: Dan Goodin article: https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2014/06/poorly-anonymized-logs-reveal-nyc-cab-drivers-detailed-whereabouts/

The result is a 173 million rows of personal information. Pandurangan's exercise ended there, but linking license number to driver name or medallion to owner are doable with resources directly from the NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission.[^4] The resulting possibilities raise clear privacy concerns: how much did a specific person make in a year, or where do they likely live are answerable questions.

[^4]: Hack license to name, NYC TLC: https://www.nyc.gov/html/tlc_medallion_info/html/tlc_lookup.shtml

No ethical boundaries were crossed in the permission structure or data collection (the same information for following years is available without a FOIL request on NYC OpenData today). Instead, the driver's privacy breach reflects a failure in anonymization and lack of care toward preparing data for public release. Further, a lack or complexity of options was not the issue; as Pandurangan suggests, the TLC could assign each driver the same, non-reversible, identifier.

Researchers, policymakers, or interested New Yorkers may be excited about the possibility for increased specificity, but these informational gains come at the cost driver privacy that was not appropriately protected: earnings, routines, and whereabouts all made public. In this specific case, the ethical violation is a result of poor data governance, not profit. Once benevolent transparency is turned into dangerous surveillance of those who produced the data in the first place.
